primary_cause: No major negative Lilly-specific news Mar 9-11. Mar 3 statement said did not anticipate shortages including insulin. Broad COVID panic hitting healthcare and pharma
secondary_factors: Defensive names sold for liquidity. Investors rotating indiscriminately despite pharma resilience profile. S&P 500 fell 9.5% on Mar 12
store_description: Lilly's 10.0% drop looks mostly like a forced-risk-off move rather than an issuer event. No meaningful negative Lilly announcement on March 9-11. Given the S&P 500's 9.5% collapse on March 12 after the WHO pandemic call Trump Europe travel ban and ECB disappointment the selloff was overwhelmingly macro.

primary_cause: COVID demand destruction fears for away-from-home beverage sales. Reuters later quantified roughly 50% of Coca-Cola revenue from restaurants theaters stadiums and away-from-home channels
secondary_factors: General market liquidation. Europe travel restrictions added to recession fears. March 12 cross-asset panic sold even consumer staples
store_description: KO's decline was likely driven by investors realizing that social distancing and venue closures threatened its fountain restaurant cinema and event exposure. Reuters later said restaurants theaters and similar venues accounted for about 50% of Coca-Cola revenue.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and cyclical tech derating on escalating COVID supply-chain and demand fears. No major Nvidia-specific corporate release Mar 9-11
secondary_factors: High-beta tech sold aggressively in March 12 liquidation. No stock-specific positive offset in preceding 3 days
store_description: Nvidia's 12.2% drop appears to have been mostly a sector-beta move tied to worsening COVID disruption fears rather than a company announcement. Investors were focused on factory interruptions semiconductor supply risk and a possible global demand shock.

primary_cause: Abrupt repricing of digital advertising revenue risk as brands cut budgets. Reuters Mar 12 reported U.S. ad industry could lose nearly $26B or 10.6%
secondary_factors: Broader market panic. Travel ban worsened expectations for travel entertainment and small-business advertisers
store_description: Facebook's 9.3% fall had a clearer stock-specific driver than many names. Reuters said the U.S. ad industry faced about $26B of lost revenue and a 10.6% decline as marketers cut spend. Since Facebook was heavily exposed to ad budgets from travel local business and brand advertisers that report likely amplified the macro selloff.

primary_cause: Macro crash overwhelmed otherwise decent earnings. Oracle reported fiscal Q3 Mar 12 — revenue $9.8B up 2% non-GAAP EPS $0.97 up 11% boosted buyback by $15B
secondary_factors: Enterprise software still faced recession risk. Investors skeptical reported numbers fully captured coming COVID hit
store_description: Oracle's 11.0% drop does not look earnings-driven in the usual sense. Oracle posted Q3 revenue of $9.8B cloud support revenue of $6.9B and non-GAAP EPS of $0.97 while authorizing $15B more in repurchases. That is broadly supportive but the report hit on the same day the S&P 500 fell 9.5%.

primary_cause: Bank-sector repricing from near-zero-rate expectations yield-curve collapse and looming credit stress. Wells carried Fed asset-cap overhang limiting balance-sheet flexibility
secondary_factors: Later asked Fed to lift growth cap to support customers underscoring issue mattered in COVID shock. No major positive WFC-specific catalyst
store_description: WFC's 15.9% decline was one of the clearest sector transmission trades. As yields collapsed and investors priced a deep recession banks were marked down for margin compression and future loan losses. Wells was hit harder because its Fed asset cap already limited balance-sheet flexibility.

primary_cause: No material negative Pfizer-specific headline Mar 9-11. Not yet COVID-vaccine winner in investors' eyes. Broad pandemic and liquidity selloff
secondary_factors: Investors selling defensives alongside cyclicals to raise cash. Concern over non-COVID business disruption
store_description: Pfizer's 6.7% drop was milder than much of the tape and appears mostly macro-driven. No major negative Pfizer issuer event in the prior 3 days. The most plausible explanation is broad liquidation after the WHO pandemic declaration Europe travel restrictions and the March 12 bear-market break.

primary_cause: Combined supply shock and demand shock in oil. Saudi-Russia price war — crude plunged ~25% on Mar 9. Mar 12 Brent fell another 7% after Trump Europe travel curbs
secondary_factors: Energy equities already under intense pressure. Investors anticipated capex cuts weaker cash flow and balance-sheet strain
store_description: XOM's 11.4% drop was very clearly oil-driven. Reuters said crude had already fallen about 25% on March 9 in the Saudi-Russia price war with Exxon suffering its biggest one-day decline since 2008 and then Brent slid another 7% on March 12 after the Europe travel restrictions.

primary_cause: Broad market panic. Concern pandemic disruption would raise labor cleaning and stocking costs even if sales rose. Not yet settled on stay-at-home winner narrative
secondary_factors: Walmart announced Mar 14 stores would move to 6am-11pm hours for restocking and cleaning. Demand surging but operations under strain
store_description: WMT's 9.1% decline looks less like a demand problem than a timing and positioning problem. By mid-March Walmart was clearly facing extraordinary demand but on March 12 the market was still in indiscriminate sell mode and worried that labor supply-chain and in-store safety pressures would overwhelm near-term sales benefit.

primary_cause: Bank-sector selloff from collapsing yields and rising recession and default expectations. Reuters later reported JPM suspended buybacks Mar 15 to preserve lending capacity
secondary_factors: Expectations of capital conservation and weaker shareholder payouts added pressure. No major JPM-specific negative issuer event
store_description: JPM's 8.2% decline was mostly a rates-and-credit story. As the market priced aggressive Fed easing and recession risk banks were sold on lower net interest margins and future loan losses. Reuters later report that JPM halted buybacks to direct capital toward lending supports the view investors were already discounting a crisis-response regime.

primary_cause: No major Verizon-specific negative Mar 9-11. Macro liquidation. Beginning to factor in retail-store disruption slower handset upgrades and weaker roaming
secondary_factors: Earlier withdrew from RSA over coronavirus in February. Investors starting to think beyond wireless service to media advertising and device activity
store_description: Verizon's 6.6% drop looks primarily like a market-wide de-risking move. No material Verizon-specific negative headline in the prior 3 days. Investors sold even defensive telecoms amid the March 12 panic while starting to anticipate store-traffic weakness and lower device activity.

primary_cause: Abrupt repricing of cross-border payments and travel-spend exposure after Europe travel restrictions. Reuters later reported rapid deterioration in cross-border travel-related spending and 4% decline in March-to-date U.S. payments volume
secondary_factors: Domestic categories like restaurants entertainment and fuel also starting to weaken sharply. No Mar 9-11 Visa company release
store_description: Visa's 7.4% decline makes sense as a direct second-order casualty of the travel ban and stay-at-home expectations. Reuters later said Visa saw rapid deterioration in cross-border travel-related spending and that U.S. payments volume was down 4% in March to date.

primary_cause: Bank-sector repricing for lower NIMs and higher credit losses. Later suspended buybacks Mar 15 reinforcing severity of stress
secondary_factors: Regional banks often trade as more credit-sensitive than money-center defensives in recession scare. No major USB-specific negative headline
store_description: USB's 12.7% drop looks like a pure financials stress trade. No obvious USB-specific bad news in the prior 3 days but as yields collapsed and recession odds rose investors marked down regionals for net interest margin compression and future credit costs.

primary_cause: Repricing of freight and industrial demand risk from global shutdowns. Fast deterioration in global trade industrial production and freight expectations
secondary_factors: Railroads caught in cyclical selloff tied to energy autos and manufacturing weakness. No Union Pacific-specific headline
store_description: UNP's 6.7% fall appears macro-cyclical rather than stock-specific. Investors were rapidly pricing weaker intermodal and industrial freight as COVID disrupted supply chains and transport networks.

primary_cause: Broad healthcare and payer uncertainty from COVID testing and treatment cost exposure layered on market panic. Insurers pledged to cover COVID testing at no cost
secondary_factors: Investors feared utilization shocks policy intervention and disrupted medical economics before it was clear that postponed elective procedures could offset some COVID costs
store_description: UNH's near-10% decline likely reflected sudden uncertainty about how much of the pandemic bill insurers would absorb. Major insurers were pledging no-cost testing and Congress was moving toward legislation requiring testing coverage while the market was still too early to see the later offset from delayed elective care.

primary_cause: Sudden collapse in expected ride demand from travel restrictions and social distancing. Mar 7 Uber said would compensate drivers diagnosed or quarantined for up to 14 days
secondary_factors: Gig-worker sick-leave and pay issues and uncertainty around support costs. Europe travel ban and pandemic declaration implied sharp fall in airport and urban mobility demand
store_description: Uber's 13.8% drop was one of the clearest business-model hits. The Europe travel ban and pandemic declaration implied a sharp fall in airport and urban mobility demand while Uber was simultaneously taking on driver-support obligations of up to 14 days of compensation for infected or quarantined workers.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and industrial demand fears from global COVID shock. Exposure to industrial and auto end-markets made it especially vulnerable
secondary_factors: TXN tapped bond market Mar 3 paying wider spreads because coronavirus volatility had disrupted issuance. No major negative TXN-specific operational announcement
store_description: TXN's 8.4% fall looks like a cyclical semiconductor repricing rather than a company event. Investors were discounting weaker industrial and automotive demand tighter financial conditions and supply-chain disruption. Even its early-March bond issuance came at meaningfully wider spreads.

primary_cause: High-beta auto and EV selloff on COVID demand destruction and factory disruption risk. Shanghai ramp disrupted earlier in February
secondary_factors: Tesla's elevated valuation and volatility made it especially vulnerable in forced deleveraging. Beginning to contemplate shutdown risk at Fremont and weaker global vehicle demand
store_description: Tesla's 11.6% drop was likely a mix of macro risk-off and very specific auto-sector COVID fear. Earlier Reuters reporting had tied coronavirus to Tesla's Shanghai production delay and delivery impact and by March 12 investors were also starting to contemplate shutdown risk at Fremont.

primary_cause: Broad market liquidation overwhelmed POSITIVE merger news. Mar 11 California and other states ended opposition to Sprint merger in settlement
secondary_factors: Investors nervous about financing and integration risk in collapsing market. Consumer and wireless retail disruption from pandemic
store_description: TMUS is one of the clearer cases where stock-specific news was actually favorable. Reuters said on March 11 that California and other states agreed to end their opposition to the Sprint deal so the 11.2% drop the next day appears to have been a pure panic-tape move.

primary_cause: No major AT&T-specific negative Mar 9-11. Broad pandemic selloff plus growing concern about AT&T media and advertising exposure
secondary_factors: Wireless retail roaming advertising and WarnerMedia all under pressure. Reuters later documented large COVID hits to AT&T media revenue and subscriber trends
store_description: AT&T's 9.2% drop was probably not driven by a single issuer event. The better explanation is that March 12 forced investors to confront COVID exposure across multiple AT&T businesses at once: wireless retail roaming advertising and WarnerMedia.
